subject: babaYagaHut
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs.
Style: Slavic folk art.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a single TypeScript module depicting Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs—scaly yellow legs with talons, a carved log cabin, shuttered window, and door, styled with Slavic folk-art ornamentation, keeping the scope focused on the subject itself.

I'm working out the dimensions and rig: a hut roughly 3m wide on 1.8m legs, with a lightly jointed skeleton for the hip, knee, and ankle so the legs can be posed. I'm calculating limb lengths and target distances so the IK chain reaches the ground properly, mimicking a chicken's bent-knee stance.

Now I'm planning the leg sweep geometry, deciding on segment counts and radius tapers, and figuring out how to place decorative ring details like torus scales along the tube without messing up the orientation.

I'll place dorsal scale plates along the surface using stick geometry at various points and angles, then move on to building toes—three forward and one back per foot—using rod-based sweeps with joints.

For toes, I'm anchoring from the ankle point and sweeping curved capsule shapes to the tips, with claw spikes attached at the end of each toe, keeping the toe radius near ground level for proper contact.

Now I'm shifting to the hut's structure above the legs: a platform at the hip height forming the floor, with walls built from stacked horizontal log cylinders alternating along x and z axes to create overhanging log-cabin corners, layered up to form the walls.

I'm adding lighter end-cap discs to each log for a finished look, with a helper function to place logs along an axis and color them by alternating wood tones per layer.

Now I'm figuring out how to handle the front wall where the door goes — logs can't just run straight through a doorway, so I'm planning to split the front wall into left and right segments around a centered door gap for the lower layers, and considering where to place a window as well.

I'm thinking a window could work nicely in the gable above the door instead of competing for wall space, with a round carved frame for a folk-style touch, while side walls get their own shuttered windows. The door itself I'll set as a recessed blue panel with ornamental red-and-white frame posts, rather than trying to cut it directly into the log geometry.

Still writing geometry logic...

Still working out roof panel dimensions and rotation angles...

Actually I like the fish-scale idea better: small round discs arranged in staggered rows across the roof slope, like folk shingle patterns. I'm defining a helper to compute each disc's position along the roof surface given its row and distance from the eave, so I can place ~108 colored discs (red, blue, green, gold alternating) across both sides.

For the base roof panels I'm adding dark wood boxes beneath the disc layer, but I need to work out the rotation carefully so the long dimension of each panel lies along the slope rather than the world axis.

Now I'm working out the gable triangles for front and back, placing them at the correct height and thickness so they fill the space under the roof slope, aligning the gable edges with the eave and ridge points so there's no gap where the roof meets the wall.

For decoration, I'm adding a round window with a sunburst motif on each gable -- a gold disc frame with a blue center, surrounded by twelve small petal shapes arranged radially like spikes.

I'm also planning carved bargeboards along the roof edges with a scalloped lower edge made from hanging pendant shapes, plus a decorative ridge ornament (konyok) resembling a horse or rooster head at the front ridge log.

Still shaping horse head outline...

I'm adding a stone chimney rising through the roof near x=-0.7, calculating its height from the roof slope, and topping it with gray icosahedra as smoke puffs. Now moving on to placing the front door.

Figuring out the door opening height so it clears enough log layers to fit a proper slab without being too short, deciding to leave a gap across layers 0 through 5.

Reconsidering proportions against the leg height, I'll trim to 9 layers so the hut isn't overly tall relative to the chicken legs, putting the door gap across layers 0-6 for a 1.3m-tall doorway and the window gap on layers 3-6 for the sides.

Now I'm pinning down exact coordinates: floor at y=2.1, platform dimensions 3.1x0.2x2.9, log layer spacing, wall top at 4.0, eaves at 4.05, ridge at 5.25, and gable apex at 5.1 with a 1.5 half-width.

Working out the roof panel geometry now, computing the eave-to-ridge slope angle (~36.3°) and panel length, then positioning panel centers and outward normals so the roof discs sit just above the panel surface.

Checking the gable apex alignment at x=0 and verifying the roof underside height matches the wall top plate at the gable edges — finding a small gap near the corners, so I'll adjust the gable base down slightly to close it.

Now I'm adding the ridge pole as a wood-colored cylinder spanning the roof length, with konyok horse-head decorations capping the ends and barge boards planned along the gable edges.

Adding pendant cones along the lower edge in alternating red/white, plus small gold discs as mid-board decoration. For the door, I'm adding platband frame planks on either side with painted dots and a lintel with small crowning spikes forming a kokoshnik-like arch.

I'm shaping the kokoshnik arch outline above the door and designing the door slab itself with dark iron straps, a golden sun ornament in the center, and a ring knob. I'm also sketching a small leaning porch ladder with two rails and rungs connecting the elevated platform to the ground, and extending the porch overhang at the front.

Now I'm working out the side window placements, adding carved platband frames and computing the vertical gap range for the openings based on the wall layer heights.

I'm positioning the shutters at x=±1.27 with gold flower details, adding a platband frame around the opening, and setting up log segment placements with varied wood-tone colors. I'm also planning a decorative painted frieze band on the front wall above the door, featuring repeating diamond motifs.

Now I'm working on the chicken legs with yellow and darker scale coloring plus dark claws, and building feathery "trouser" fluff above them using cones and a scaled sphere at the hip with a ring of spike feathers pointing down and back.

For the rest pose I'm splaying the legs slightly, setting hip and foot x-offsets and computing IK targets and chain lengths for each leg joint, naming the joints hip/knee/ankle per side with L/R suffixes based on sign. I'm parenting the leg chains to the hip joint and sweeping a tapered mesh along each chain for the leg geometry.

Now I'm adding an ankle knob sphere and using along() to stick small embedded boxes at intervals as toe/foot details, then building the toes by projecting outward directions from the ankle point at angled offsets to place toe tips.

For the leg chain I'm passing a single bend direction for the inner joint, and confirming the limb function returns the hip position as the root so the joint placement stays correct under the platform.

Now I'm adding underside cross beams along the platform, plus a rod axle connecting the two hips for structure. Since this is a diorama, I'm also thinking about adding a simple round earth base with grass, moss, and maybe some mushrooms or flowers to ground the hut on legs.

For flair, I want a small fence of pointed stakes topped with glowing skulls -- iconic touch, maybe five posts arranged in an arc out front, each with jaw and glowing orange eye details. I also realize I need to recalculate the ground height so the lowest feet touch y=0 properly, raising the base and offsetting everything accordingly.

I'll keep hips at 2.0 and target the foot near 0.26, which still works fine with leg lengths of 1.0 each. For the base, I'm defining a lathed outline that tapers outward slightly before leveling into a grass-colored top layer over an earthy brown body.

Then I'm layering two lathes for the ground—a dirt base and a slightly offset grass ring on top—to avoid visible gaps, and scattering small cone-shaped grass tufts, a few flowers, mushrooms (cylinder stems with hemisphere caps, red with white dots), and grey icosahedron stones around the scene. I'm also positioning a skull fence along an arc in front of the hut, near where the porch ladder sits.

Placing fence posts...

Now I'm planning smoke puffs, chimney details, and settling on a color palette with deep reds, blues, and gold tones for the scene.

I'm setting up the builder structure for the hut, defining the root joint and a hinged joint for the door so it can swing open, with the shutters kept simple and attached directly to the hut body.

I'm writing a helper function to simplify placing parts bound to the hut joint with configurable position and orientation, plus a log-cylinder helper for building the walls.

Now I'm looping through the log courses, alternating wood colors and figuring out whether front/back segments need to be split around the doorway or run full length, while sides stay a fixed length.

I'll limit the end caps to front and back only to keep the part count reasonable, then add some moss lumps near the wall tops and log gaps for texture, and work out the roof disc rows and column spacing for coverage.

For the shingle layout, I'm staggering alternating rows with a z-offset so columns interlock, and I need to slightly raise each row's normal offset so lower rows sit above upper ones, mimicking real overlapping shingles and avoiding coplanar z-fighting between adjacent discs.

Still working out the grid spacing...

Still planning roof details...

For the chimney, I'm positioning it on the roof slope with brick coloring and lighter mortar bands, topped with a dark cap and small smoke puffs rising above it.

Now I'm working out the door opening between the logs, sizing it to fit the gap and positioning a flush door slab with hinge placement at the log joint.

Designing the door's decorative elements too—a central gold sun ornament with red petals, iron strap bands with rivets, a torus handle opposite the hinge, flanking frame posts, and a kokoshnik-style lintel above.

Now I'm adding a ladder leaning against the porch, with paired bone-colored rails and evenly spaced rungs connecting them, positioned so its base sits just above the floor level.

For the platform itself, I'm making a dark wood deck box and considering decorative skirting along its edges—small alternating red/white blocks lining the front edge like painted teeth, deciding whether to extend this detail to all four sides or just the front and sides for simplicity.

I'm roughly tallying total part counts across logs, roof, door, windows, gables, legs, and base elements to estimate around 560 parts, so I need to write helper functions to keep the code efficient rather than listing every piece manually. Defining window geometry now...

Adding the window frame now: red side posts, a kokoshnik-shaped extruded top arch, a blue sill below, and small gold accent dots on the posts.

Now I'm placing shutters flanking the posts and designing a flower motif for each—gold centers with petals arranged radially—so I'm building a reusable bloom helper that takes a center point, normal, and two tangent vectors to position the petals correctly.

Writing bloom helper...

I notice the rays could poke through the gable edges at the upper radius, so I'm repositioning the sunburst center lower, around y=4.4, checking that ray tips stay within the triangle's shrinking half-width at each height. I'm also confirming the lowered circle doesn't dip below the wall top, since the log courses still support it.

For decoration I'm adding a thin painted frieze band on the front wall between courses 7 and 8, with small rotated diamond shapes and gold dots spaced along it, making sure it sits clear of the door opening above.

Now for the legs I'm adding feather trouser clusters at the hips — a scaled cream-ochre sphere plus a ring of ten downward-angled cone spikes per leg using the spike helper, attached to the leg's hip joint.

I'm also adding a backward-pointing spur spike at each ankle for a claw-like detail. With the skull posts, mushrooms, grass tufts, and rocks planned, I'm now starting the actual code, importing THREE and the builder utilities and setting up typed vector helpers.

Writing imports and setup...

Defining the options type for part placement and setting up small geometry helper functions for boxes, cylinders, and spheres to simplify building hut pieces.

For the legs, I'm mapping over left/right sides to compute hip and foot positions, then using a limb helper to generate joint points along each leg and building a bone chain from them, choosing a polyline path instead of catmull-rom so the joints land exactly on the specified points.

Writing sweep geometry code...

I'm adding knee and ankle knob spheres along the bone chain, then writing a toe-generation loop that computes angled toe positions and tips from the foot point using trigonometry.

Still refining toe geometry...

Adjusting toe heights so the sweep radius doesn't clip into the foot, then adding a claw spike extending from each toe tip.

Now I'm setting up the ankle joint reference and sketching the door hinge joint attached to the hut, placing it near the frame edge with a vertical hinge direction.

Still writing door geometry...

Still writing bloom geometry...

Now I'm working out the gable ends, placing extruded plates on both front and back at symmetric z-offsets, colored in a weathered wood tone, with a decorative sun disc mounted on the surface above each gable.

Adding sun rays and frame ring...

I'm verifying the panel's orientation lines up with the slope correctly, then checking the disc rows along the ridge — the spacing puts the last disc slightly past the ridge line, so I need to adjust the radius or position to avoid overlap with the ridge pole.

Adjusting disc spacing and sizing...

Now I'm setting up the disc colors by cycling through a folk palette, and sketching the bargeboard trim pieces along both roof edges with a cream-colored box.

Adding pendant cones and gold discs along the boards, trimming the counts down to 8 each to keep part totals reasonable, then starting the ridge pole as a wood cylinder centered at the peak.

Placing the eye near the head region and adding a few gold mane cones along the back-of-neck curve, plus a red nostril sphere. I'm positioning the konyok on the pole so it hangs forward past the roof edge, checking its base height and vertical extent fit within the pole's top.

Reconsidering: the konyok should really be a flat carved plate seen in side profile at the gable end, lying along the ridge rather than sticking forward. I'm repositioning it so the plate sits embedded in the pole near the ridge top, with the neck rising above the pole surface.

I'm also adding gold sphere finials at the pole ends, finishing the chimney and smoke, and building the platform box with underbeam cylinders along the hip points plus a connecting axle rod, checking that everything clears below the beam height.

Now I'm laying out skirt blocks alternating red and white around the platform's front, sides, and back edges, computing roughly 38 total block positions, then considering trimming the side count down. I'll also plan some moss details on the roof and walls, skipping a few to keep things simpler.

Then I'm writing the base using lathe shapes for the dirt mound and grass topper, defining the outline points and checking that the fence radius stays within the platform bounds.

Next I'm scattering grass tufts randomly across the ground using cones in varying greens, adding a dozen small flowers with stems and colored blooms, and placing a few mushrooms near the base at specific coordinates.

Each mushroom gets a cream stem with a flattened red half-dome cap dotted in white, plus I'm adding flattened grey icosahedron rocks nearby. Then I'm setting up the skull posts with stake-like cylinders and small skull spheres mounted at the top.

Now I'm placing jawbone, eyes, and nose details on the skull, trying to figure out orientation so the jaw box aligns with the tangent direction, and settling on a small cylinder shape instead for simplicity.

With the skull facing outward handled, I'm turning to the smoke effect above the hut—stacking a few grey icosahedron spheres at increasing height and size to simulate rising smoke, keeping the total structure under roughly 7.3 units tall. I'm also deciding to skip adding a matching frieze on the back and considering whether to add moss detailing.

Now I'm adding small moss patches on a few of the roof sections, then moving on to writing out the door frame details—red wooden posts flanking the entrance with decorative white dot studs, sized so the inner edges leave a clean gap for the doorway, plus a lintel piece above.

Adding the kokoshnik arch...

I'm checking the frieze position for collisions with the kokoshnik and deciding to split it into two side boards instead of one continuous strip to avoid overlap.

Now I'm planning the actual extrude calls and part placements, working out how local coordinates on each frame map into model space for positioning the eye spheres on the head.

Still mapping out mane cones along the back edge, confirming the stick and spike function signatures before finalizing the build code.

I'm checking sweep options for the chain-based tube sections and glow wrapping on parts, then nailing down the fluff and claw colors for the final detail pass.

Writing final assembly code...
